Imagine you and your friends want to keep track of who owes whom money. Instead of using a single notebook, you all agree to write down every transaction on a big shared list. She had been alone for weeks—since the accident. Her husband, Martin, had been taken from her in a sudden car crash that left her with nothing but guilt and a fractured leg that would take months to heal. The doctors had said she was lucky to be alive. But luck, she realized, had nothing to do with it. Survival was more about will than fate.

Her eyes drifted to the photo on the wall—Martin smiling, his arm around her, their dog, Max, catching a ball in the background. The memory was a balm and a wound all at once. Sarah’s heart froze. She had been alone for so long that the sound of a footstep felt like a ghost. She forced herself to move, her leg throbbing with each step. She crept toward the kitchen, her breath shallow, her pulse a drumbeat in her ears.

She found him there—Max. Her dog. He was limping, soaked, and shivering, his fur matted with rain and leaves. He looked up at her with eyes full of sorrow and relief.
